metadata.title: Recommendations for Reducing the Risk of Transfusion-Transmitted Hepatitis B Virus: Guidance for Industry
metadata.topic: Guidance · FDA human drugs and biologics
metadata.legal_basis: FDA Guidance Document (21 CFR 10.115). Guidance states FDA's current thinking and is not binding unless a statute or regulation requires it; the official text governs.

candidates.statement: Under 21 CFR 610.40(a)(1), an establishment that collects blood and blood components must test each donation of human blood or blood components for transfusion or for use in manufacturing a product, including donations intended as a component of, or used to manufacture, a medical device, for evidence of infection due to HBV. In addition, under 21 CFR 610.40(b), establishments must use, in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions, one or more screening tests that FDA has licensed, approved or cleared as necessary to meet the testing requirement and to reduce adequately and appropriately the risk of transmission of RTTIs. This guidance provides recommendations for testing blood donations to reduce adequately and appropriately the risk of HBV transmission under these regulations.
candidates.context: HBV is a relevant transfusion-transmitted infection (RTTI) (Title 21 of the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) 630.3(h)(1)(ii)) and, therefore, subject to the testing requirements in 21 CFR 610.40, the donor deferral requirements in 21 CFR 610.41 and the donor notification requirements in 21 CFR 630.40. candidates.statement: Additionally, we have revised some recommendations because of advances in the tests used to screen blood donations for HBV. We removed recommendations that blood establishments use HBsAg and HBV NAT tests with specific sensitivity levels, as described in the November 2007 and October 2012 Final Guidance documents. These recommendations are no longer relevant because all currently available FDA-licensed tests for HBsAg and HBV DNA meet the detection levels previously recommended and blood establishments must use FDA-licensed, approved or cleared screening tests in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions (see 21 CFR 610.40(b)). Further, we have made minor changes in recommendations for donor requalification and product management for consistency and alignment with current practice.

In general, FDA’s guidance documents do not establish legally enforceable responsibilities.

candidates.statement: B. FDA Regulatory History FDA first recommended testing for HBV in December 1987. In a memorandum addressed to all registered blood establishments, FDA recommended testing each donation for HBsAg using an FDA-licensed test and that an HBsAg-reactive unit should not be used for transfusion or further manufacturing use. The December 1987 memo also recommended using an FDA-licensed confirmatory (neutralization) test for HBsAg to evaluate donors whose donation tested repeatedly reactive. FDA provided recommendations for evaluating the status of the donor, including that the donor should be permanently deferred when the HBsAg confirmatory test is positive by neutralization. If the HBsAg reactivity in the donor’s sample is not neutralizable (i.e., not confirmed positive), the memo recommended testing for anti-HBc with an FDA- approved test. If repeatedly reactive for anti-HBc, the donor is permanently deferred; if not reactive, then the donor should be deferred for 8 weeks, and the subsequent donation should be tested for HBsAg and anti-HBc to determine donor eligibility and donation suitability.
candidates.context: The risk of posttransfusion hepatitis was recognized in the 1940s, but the etiology was unknown for many years. In the 1960s, posttransfusion hepatitis was reported in up to 1.5% of transfusion recipients (Ref. 7). HBsAg was identified to be associated with HBV infection in 1970, and HBsAg assays became the first to screen blood donations for a viral infection. Subsequent improvements in blood donor screening assays resulted in detection of early or acute viral markers (HBsAg, HBV DNA) and chronic infection (anti-HBc) in plasma and serum. On average, HBsAg becomes detectable 30 days after exposure (with a range of 6-60 days), while HBV DNA can be detected 10-20 days earlier (Ref. 8). Anti-HBc appears after HBV DNA and HBsAg and persists for life in most infected individuals (Ref. 9). candidates.statement: On February 20, 1990, FDA announced in the Federal Register that, effective March 31, 1991, total anti-HBc test kits used for the purpose of screening blood donations would be regulated as licensed biological products. In September 1991, in a memorandum to all registered blood establishments, FDA recommended that all donations of blood and blood components intended for transfusion be screened by an FDA-licensed anti-HBc test in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions. The memo recommended that a repeatedly reactive donation should not be used for transfusion and that donors who tested repeatedly reactive for anti-HBc on more than one occasion should be deferred. The memo provided recommendations for labeling and quarantine and disposition of repeatedly reactive donations.

candidates.statement: In a July 1996 memo to blood establishments, FDA provided recommendations for the quarantine and disposition of blood, blood components, and Source Plasma from prior collections from donors with repeatedly reactive screening tests for HBV. The July 1996 memo recommended that blood and plasma establishments should identify and quarantine such donations in their inventory within one week and notify consignees to quarantine components that had been distributed. The memo provided recommendations for the disposition of units placed in quarantine based on the result of further testing of the initially reactive donation.

The memo clarified that recovered plasma donations may be shipped for further manufacture under a valid short supply agreement regardless of the anti-HBc test results. FDA issued guidance in November 2007 that recommended minimum sensitivity standards for HBsAg tests for the purpose of blood donation screening. The guidance recommended that blood establishments use HBsAg assays that have a lower limit of detection capability of 0.5 nanograms (ng) HBsAg/mL or less. The guidance also provided test kit manufacturers with a recommended performance standard when testing the CBER HBsAg Lot-Release Panel #12 under 21 CFR 610.44.

candidates.statement: In May 2010, with the availability of FDA-licensed NAT for HBV DNA and improved sensitivity of licensed total anti-HBc tests, FDA provided recommendations for a requalification method for donors deferred because of falsely positive repeatedly reactive test results for anti- HBc on more than one occasion. The guidance recommended that after an eight-week period, a follow-up pre-donation sample from the donor should be tested for HBsAg, anti-HBc and HBV DNA by NAT (with a sensitivity of <2 IU/mL at 95 % detection rate) using FDA-licensed tests.
candidates.context: FDA issued guidance in November 2007 that recommended minimum sensitivity standards for HBsAg tests for the purpose of blood donation screening. The guidance recommended that blood establishments use HBsAg assays that have a lower limit of detection capability of 0.5 nanograms (ng) HBsAg/mL or less. The guidance also provided test kit manufacturers with a recommended performance standard when testing the CBER HBsAg Lot-Release Panel #12 under 21 CFR 610.44. Negative results on all three tests in the follow-up sample qualified the donor for reentry. The May 2010 guidance also recommended continued indefinite deferral of the donor if the follow- up sample tested repeatedly reactive on the HBsAg or anti-HBc test or reactive on the HBV NAT.

candidates.statement: In May 2015, FDA issued a final rule titled, “Requirements for Blood and Blood Components Intended for Transfusion or for Further Manufacturing Use” (the “Donor Eligibility” rule, 80 FR 29841). Among other things, the rulemaking defined RTTI as including HBV in 21 CFR 630.3(h)(1)(ii)) and codified that each donation of blood and blood components for transfusion or for use in manufacturing a product must be tested for evidence of HBV (21 CFR 610.40(a)(1)). The 2015 final rule clarified that when a donation tests reactive on a screening test for an RTTI, including HBV, you must perform further testing as described in 21 CFR 610.40(e); the donation is not suitable for release unless an exception applies (21 CFR 630.30(b)); and, the donor must be deferred (21 CFR 610.41) and notified of the reason for deferral (21 CFR 630.40).
candidates.context: For donation screening, the October 2012 guidance recommended use of an FDA-licensed NAT for HBV DNA with a lower limit of detection of < 100 IU/mL HBV DNA for HBV DNA detection in an individual donation of blood and blood components for transfusion, and <500 IU/mL HBV DNA for HBV DNA detection in an individual donation of Source Plasma. The guidance clarified that screening with a licensed NAT for HBV DNA could be in minipool donation-sample testing format or an individual donation testing format and may include multiplex NAT with testing of other agents, such as HIV and HCV. The guidance also recommended further testing of donations reactive for HBsAg with an FDA-licensed NAT for HBV DNA with a supplemental testing indication or HBsAg neutralization to meet the requirement of 21 CFR 610.40(e).
